extracted.intended_audience: readers of literary/historical criticism and students of political/biographical analysis
extracted.subtask_description: A literary-historical essay arguing for a reconsideration of Oliver Cromwell's character and leadership, describing criteria by which to judge 'great men' (silence, virtue, sincerity, ambition, leadership) and defending Cromwell against charges of hypocrisy. The text offers evaluative principles for assessing historical figures' motives and actions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intellect judged by insight, not oratory
rubrics_metrics.description: Intellect is not speaking and logicizing; it is seeing and ascertaining.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate a man's intellect by his capacity to 'see' and ascertain truth rather than by polished speech or rhetorical skill. Anti-pattern: discounting someone because they are ineloquent; scoring should favor demonstrable insight over verbal fluency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Virtue / hero-hood as Tugend (doing and courage)
rubrics_metrics.description: Virtue, Virtues, manhood, hero-hood, is... what the Germans well name it, Tugend (Taugend, dow-ing or Dough-tiness), Courage and the Faculty to do.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess moral greatness by practical courage and the ability to act ('the Faculty to do'), not by 'fair-spoken immaculate regularity.' Preference is given to effectiveness and moral firmness over rhetorical or cosmetic virtue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prophetic/inarticulate greatness
rubrics_metrics.description: Prophetic men may be 'inarticulate'—'Prophet who could not speak'—yet possess inner clarity, sympathy, and depth that promise mastery over things.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Don't treat confused or rhapsodic speech as evidence of lack of inner meaning. Examples: Cromwell's reputed confusion of speech can coexist with deep inward conviction. Scoring should allow for extempore prayer, rhapsodic preaching, and other non-methodical utterances as genuine signs of conviction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prayer as a legitimate method of arriving at purpose
rubrics_metrics.description: The devout, prostrating, earnest struggling soul prays for guidance; 'All his great enterprises were commenced with prayer.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing motives and decisions in religious/pious actors, consider prayer and devout deliberation as authentic processes for forming purpose (not mere hypocrisy). Anti-pattern: dismissing religious deliberation as mere theatrics without examining its fruits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reticence and guardedness are not hypocrisy
rubrics_metrics.description: Superior men must have reticences; 'There is no use for any man's taking up his abode in a house built of glass.' A man judges how much of his mind to show.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish wise dissimulation (keeping prudent things private to accomplish aims) from moral lying. Penalize deliberate deception intended to mislead; do not penalize prudent secrecy or withholding of full plans from every inquirer.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep course and starting-point in view (don't substitute goal for course)
rubrics_metrics.description: It is an error to substitute the goal of a man's career for the course and starting-point of it; vulgar history presumes a pre-set program which the actor did not foresee.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate historical actors by reconstructing their actual sequence of choices and contingencies rather than reading backward from later outcomes as if premeditated. Anti-pattern: attributing a lifelong preformed program to actions that arose contingently.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish two kinds of ambition
rubrics_metrics.description: There are two kinds of ambition; one wholly blamable (prurient, craving notice) and the other laudable and inevitable (the urge to unfold one's natural capacities and serve duties).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge ambition by motive and fitness: penalize self-seeking, attention-hungry ambition; reward ambition that aims to fulfill a genuine capacity or public good. Consider whether the person's nature and calling justify seeking the position.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate ambition by fitness for office and quality of purpose
rubrics_metrics.description: To decide about ambition... Not the coveting of the place alone, but the fitness of the man for the place withal: that is the question.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing whether seeking power is blameworthy, weigh the individual's aptitude and the potential public benefit. Example: Mirabeau's seeking premiership might be justified if he alone could have helped France.

rubrics_metrics.name: Silence as a positive virtue ('Empire of Silence')
rubrics_metrics.description: Silence, the great Empire of Silence: higher than the stars; deeper than the Kingdoms of Death! It alone is great; all else is small.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value quiet, contemplative, non-public-producing greatness. Anti-pattern: equating visibility and spectacle with worth; prefer long-term private labors and rooted thought over showy public display.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ability to keep one's mind to oneself as a practical necessity
rubrics_metrics.description: He that cannot withal keep his mind to himself cannot practice any considerable thing whatever.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess leaders' prudence by their capacity to avoid revealing all plans to every questioner; penalize indiscriminate candour that undermines effective action. This is a practical, not moral, criterion (distinguishing between secrecy for prudence vs. secrecy for malice).

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not conflate rhetorical form with moral reality (speeches may appear chaotic but contain meaning)
rubrics_metrics.description: Cromwell's printed speeches, though 'shapeless, involved chaotic,' can contain a real speech imprisoned in broken utterances; reporters were candid and left what they heard.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When using textual speeches as evidence, consider context, delivery, and intent; fragmented or unadorned speech may reveal genuine conviction. Anti-pattern: treating lack of rhetorical polish as evidence of insincerity or intellectual poverty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sincerity should be judged by persistent purpose and final acts
rubrics_metrics.description: Sincere hero hearts do not sink into mere hypocrisy; the Sun may be dimmed but not extinguished. Cromwell's last prayers and broken words show a Christian heroic man.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate claims of hypocrisy by looking for long-term continuity of motive, conduct in extremis (e.g., deathbed utterances), and the balance of faults to core commitments. Avoid simplistic 'became a hypocrite' narratives without nuanced evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Leadership requires a decisive 'Chief' — necessity over formula
rubrics_metrics.description: Indispensable everywhere a King is, in all movements of men... Subjects without a King can do nothing; a subjectless King can do something.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In judging historical political actions, weigh the practical need for a decisive leader against constitutional/formalist objections. Where collective bodies are paralysed, the emergence of a single capable chief may be a necessary (if anomalous) remedy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contextual judgement of extraordinary assumption of power
rubrics_metrics.description: When parliaments could not act and anarchy or despotism were alternatives, accepting Protectorship may be judged as preventing anarchy: 'there was no alternative but Anarchy or that.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess extraordinary grabs for authority by contextual consequences and available alternatives rather than by abstract labels like 'usurpation.' Consider whether the act preserved order or served public good; anti-pattern: condemning power assumption out of hand without contextual analysis.
